lesson.title: The Stopband: Where a Filter Does Its Job
lesson.summary: The stopband is the frequency region beyond cutoff where output falls more than 3 dB below maximum and keeps falling, the region a filter is built to suppress.
lesson.body:
If the passband is where a filter's frequency response stays close to its maximum, the stopband is everything past the point where that promise breaks down. By convention, the stopband begins where the magnitude falls more than 3 dB below maximum, meaning it starts exactly at the far side of the half power point, and it keeps going, with attenuation continuing to increase as frequency moves further from the passband.

Unlike the passband, where loss stays small and gradual, the stopband is defined by loss that keeps compounding. For a single pole low pass filter, once you are past cutoff, every additional factor of 10 in frequency, one decade, adds roughly another 20 dB of attenuation. This is not a coincidence; it is the same slope that shows up later in the asymptotic approximation chapter when the frequency response is sketched as straight lines on a log log plot.

Check this with the same resistor capacitor filter used in the last two chapters, R equals 1000 ohms, C equals 0.1 microfarads, cutoff frequency f_c equals 1591.5 Hz. Move one decade above cutoff, to f equals 15,915 Hz, so the ratio f over f_c equals 10. The magnitude is 1 over the square root of 1 plus 10 squared, which is 1 over the square root of 101, or 1 divided by 10.0499, giving 0.09950. In decibels, 20 log10(0.09950) equals negative 20.04 dB. That is a power ratio of roughly 1 part in 100, a dramatic drop compared with the mild negative 0.41 dB loss found inside the passband one chapter ago. This is exactly what a stopband is supposed to do: not just attenuate, but attenuate aggressively and progressively the further a frequency strays from where it belongs.

The border between passband and stopband is not a wall; it is the single half power point studied at the start of this unit, and the width of the region on the passing side of that border is what the next chapter measures directly as bandwidth.
